title: Building a TOK Journal That Actually Helps Later
summary: Build a practical TOK journal from September to November that captures examples, questions and reflections you can reuse for the exhibition and essay.
body_markdown:
Building a TOK journal helps later only if it records **usable thinking** , not summaries of every lesson. During the September-to-November fall term, it should become a searchable collection of real-world examples, knowledge questions, competing perspectives, and reflections on how claims are justified.


A TOK journal is not an official assessed component. The IB assesses TOK through the **exhibition** and the **1,600-word essay** , as explained in the[official IB overview of Theory of Knowledge](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/curriculum/dp-core/theory-of-knowledge/) . However, a well-designed journal develops the examples and analytical habits needed for both tasks.


### What a TOK journal is actually for


The journal should help you notice TOK outside the classroom. News stories, subject lessons, personal experiences, cultural disagreements, and methodological problems can all become material for examining how knowledge is produced, acquired, or communicated.


A useful journal performs four functions:


- **Captures examples** before important details are forgotten
- **Develops knowledge questions** from specific situations
- **Records contrasting perspectives** instead of one-sided opinions
- **Builds analytical habits** that transfer to assessed work


The journal is usually a teacher-recommended formative tool, not an IB submission requirement. Your school may set its own expectations, so follow the format and schedule established by your TOK teacher.


### Use a structure that produces reusable material


Avoid treating the journal as a diary of classroom activities. Each entry should move from a specific situation to a broader question about knowledge.


Entry component What to record


Situation A specific event, object, claim, experiment, text, or disagreement


Source and context Where it came from, when it appeared, and who produced it


Knowledge issue A problem involving evidence, certainty, values, authority, or interpretation


Knowledge question An open, debatable question about knowledge itself


Perspectives At least two reasonable approaches to the question


Evaluation Which view is stronger, under what conditions, and why


This reflects skills identified in the[official IB TOK subject brief](https://ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/programmes/dp/pdfs/tok-sb-english.pdf) , including examining knowledge questions, evaluating viewpoints, using examples, and considering implications.


For example, suppose a medical study is challenged because its participant sample was too narrow. Do not merely summarize the study and state that biased samples are harmful. Ask: **Under what conditions does limited evidence justify a general knowledge claim?** One perspective may demand strict standards before generalization; another may argue that decisions sometimes must be made before complete evidence exists. Your evaluation might conclude that the appropriate standard depends partly on the consequences of being wrong.


### A September-to-November routine


One deliberate entry each week is more useful than several rushed summaries. The aim is to create a varied bank of material before coursework deadlines narrow your attention.


### September: establish the habit


Notice situations in which people disagree about what is true, justified, reliable, or worth knowing. Draw examples from your DP subjects, community, experiences, and carefully selected current events.


Spend **10-15 minutes** recording the context, then about **10 minutes** developing a knowledge question and two perspectives. The[RevisionDojo guide to TOK knowledge questions](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/examples-and-tips-for-writing-ib-tok-knowledge-questions) can help if your questions remain factual rather than focusing on knowledge.


### October: organize and connect


Tag every entry with two or three consistent labels, such as an **area of knowledge** , a TOK concept, and a possible exhibition theme. Avoid creating so many categories that retrieval becomes difficult.


Look for comparisons between entries. Historical testimony and laboratory measurement may both raise questions about reliability, but each area of knowledge resolves uncertainty differently. Such comparisons can later support more precise essay arguments.


### November: review for quality


Identify your five strongest examples and improve their context, source details, counterarguments, and implications. Ask whether each example reveals a genuine knowledge tension, can be explained without restarting the research, and could support more than one argument.


This review turns disconnected notes into a working resource. The[RevisionDojo TOK resource hub](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-theory-of-knowledge-tok) can help you connect entries to important concepts and assessments.


### Preparing for the TOK exhibition


The exhibition uses three objects connected to one official prompt. It explores how TOK manifests in the world around us and contributes **33%** of the TOK result.


Treat your journal as an object-candidate bank. When an entry involves a photograph, document, message, tool, annotation, data display, or personal possession, record the exact object and its **specific real-world context** . Instead of writing “a newspaper article,” record its title, publication, date, relevant claim, and why you encountered it.


Use the[TOK exhibition prompt guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/tok-exhibition-prompts-b4a14cd7) to compare possible connections, but do not force every entry into a prompt. Preserve several possibilities until you can judge which objects support the most convincing analysis.


### Preparing for the TOK essay


The essay is an externally assessed response to one of six prescribed titles issued for the relevant examination session. Because titles change between sessions, your journal should collect adaptable material rather than attempt to predict a future title.


For each strong example, add a short **transfer note** containing:


- Relevant areas of knowledge and TOK concepts
- A possible claim and counterclaim
- Conditions under which each position is convincing
- Limitations of the example


An example is useful only when you explain how it supports, qualifies, or challenges an argument about knowledge. When titles are released for your cohort, consult the[RevisionDojo TOK essay hub](https://www.revisiondojo.com/tok-hub) and verify their exact wording. Never alter a prescribed title to fit material already collected.


### Digital or handwritten?


Choose the format that lets you retrieve and compare entries months later.


Format Main advantage Main limitation


Digital Searchable, taggable, and easy to link to sources Can encourage copying without reflection


Handwritten Supports slower, deliberate thinking Harder to search and reorganize


Hybrid Combines reflection with a searchable index Requires consistent updating


For handwriting, number entries and reserve several pages for an index listing concepts, areas of knowledge, and examples. Digitally, use consistent tags instead of an elaborate folder system.


### Common mistakes


The first mistake is **summarizing content without examining knowledge** . “We learned about historical sources” records a lesson; “When does corroboration make testimony reliable?” begins an analysis.


The second is saving links without context. Record the author, date, central claim, and exact detail that raised a TOK question. This protects the usefulness of an entry if the source changes or disappears.


The third is relying on vague, famous controversies. Use an example only when you understand its facts and can connect it precisely to an argument. The[RevisionDojo collection of TOK questions and topics](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/sample-tok-questions-and-topics-for-ib-students) can help you distinguish genuine analysis from a broad social issue.


Finally, do not let AI write your reflections. Jojo AI can suggest an opposing interpretation or test whether a question is open-ended, but the journal should preserve your judgment and comply with your school's academic integrity rules.


### Entry checklist


Before completing an entry, confirm that it includes:


- A specific, accurately recorded situation
- Enough source information to find it later
- An open knowledge question
- At least two plausible perspectives
- Your evaluation of conditions and limitations
- Relevant tags and a possible assessment use


### Conclusion


A TOK journal becomes valuable when it supports retrieval, comparison, and evaluation. From September to November, write one structured entry each week, preserve precise contexts, develop knowledge questions, and review your strongest material.


RevisionDojo TOK Study Notes and exhibition resources can clarify concepts, while Jojo AI can help test counterclaims after you have completed your own analysis.
